questions.commandDemand: Give the cause and the process. Do not stop at what you saw; say what caused it and name the process.
questions.stimulus: A puddle on the road disappears after a hot afternoon.
questions.stem: Explain why the puddle disappeared. Explain also why an identical puddle in a shaded, sheltered corner would still be there at the end of the afternoon.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the water evaporated
the water gained heat energy from the sun
it changed into water vapour

chain.text: Water in the puddle gained heat energy from the sun.
The water evaporated, changing from the liquid state to water vapour.
The water vapour escaped into the air, so the puddle disappeared.
The shaded puddle gained less heat energy and the sheltered air did not carry the water vapour away, so its rate of evaporation was much lower.

questions.modelAnswer: Water in the puddle gained heat energy from the sun. This caused the water to evaporate, changing from the liquid state into water vapour, which escaped into the surrounding air, so the puddle disappeared. The puddle in the shaded corner gained much less heat energy because it was not in direct sunlight, and the still air there did not carry the water vapour away. Both of these lower the rate of evaporation, so far less water evaporated and the puddle was still there at the end of the afternoon.
markPoints: Water gained heat energy from the sun
Water evaporated / changed from liquid to water vapour
The shaded puddle gained less heat energy
Still, sheltered air does not carry water vapour away, so the rate of evaporation is lower
questions.whyMarksLost: Four marks means the second half of the question is worth as much as the first. Answers that explain the sunny puddle beautifully and then write one line about shade throw away half the marks.

questions.commandDemand: Give the cause and the process behind the observation.
questions.stimulus: Water droplets form on the outside of a glass of iced water left on a table.
questions.stem: Explain how the water droplets formed on the outside of the glass.

fuzzyTraps.vague: water came out of the glass
fuzzyTraps.precise: water vapour in the air condensed on the glass
the water vapour lost heat energy to the cold glass

chain.text: Water vapour in the surrounding air touches the cold surface of the glass.
The water vapour loses heat energy to the colder glass and condenses.
It changes into liquid water, forming droplets on the outside of the glass.

questions.modelAnswer: Water vapour in the surrounding air came into contact with the cold surface of the glass. The water vapour lost heat energy to the colder glass and condensed, changing from the gaseous state into liquid water. This formed droplets on the outside of the glass.
markPoints: Water vapour in the air loses heat to the cold glass
Water vapour condenses / changes from gas to liquid
questions.whyMarksLost: A very common wrong answer is that the water leaked through the glass. The examiner wants the source named as water vapour in the air, and the process named as condensation.

questions.commandDemand: State what will happen, then give the reason. A prediction without a reason scores half.
questions.stimulus: Two identical dishes hold 50 ml of water each. Dish A is left in a shaded corner. Dish B is left beside a sunny window. Both are checked after four hours.
questions.stem: Predict which dish will contain less water after four hours, explain your answer, and state one thing that must be kept the same for this to be a fair test.

fuzzyTraps.vague: B loses more because it is hotter
fuzzyTraps.precise: B receives more heat energy, so the rate of evaporation is higher

chain.text: Dish B will contain less water.
Dish B receives more heat energy from the sunlight.
More heat energy increases the rate of evaporation.
The starting volume of water, and the size and shape of the dish, must be the same.

questions.modelAnswer: Dish B will contain less water. Dish B receives more heat energy from the sunlight than Dish A, and the greater the heat energy gained, the higher the rate of evaporation, so more water in Dish B evaporates in the same four hours. For this to be a fair test, the starting volume of water and the size and shape of the two dishes must be kept the same, so that only the amount of sunlight differs.
markPoints: Dish B contains less water
Dish B gains more heat energy, so its rate of evaporation is higher
A named variable kept the same, such as starting volume or dish size
questions.whyMarksLost: The fair-test mark is free if you name a variable and say it must be the same. Naming the thing being changed instead of a control is the usual slip.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens, in order. No reasons needed, but the sequence must be complete and in the right order.
questions.stem: Describe how water from the sea ends up falling as rain, and explain what causes the water vapour to condense as it rises.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the water evaporates and the water vapour rises

fuzzyTraps.vague: clouds get heavy and drop water
fuzzyTraps.precise: the water droplets combine until they are heavy enough to fall as rain

chain.text: Water at the sea surface gains heat energy from the sun and evaporates into water vapour.
The water vapour rises into the air.
Higher up the surroundings are colder, so the water vapour loses heat energy.
Losing heat energy makes it condense into tiny water droplets, which collect to form clouds.
The droplets combine until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.

questions.modelAnswer: Water at the surface of the sea gains heat energy from the sun and evaporates, changing into water vapour. The water vapour rises into the air. Higher up, the surroundings are much colder, so the water vapour loses heat energy to them. Losing this heat energy causes the water vapour to condense, changing back from the gaseous state into tiny droplets of liquid water, which collect together to form clouds. The droplets keep combining until they become heavy enough to fall to the ground as rain.
markPoints: Evaporation of sea water into water vapour using heat energy from the sun
The water vapour rises
Higher up it is colder, so the water vapour loses heat energy
It condenses into tiny water droplets, forming clouds
Droplets combine and become heavy enough to fall as rain
questions.whyMarksLost: The mark that decides this question is why condensation happens at all. Saying the vapour 'turns into clouds' describes it; saying it loses heat energy to the colder surroundings explains it.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a sensible method or reason. There may be more than one right answer, but it must be practical and it must work.
questions.stimulus: A family hangs wet laundry indoors on a rainy day. The clothes take a very long time to dry.
questions.stem: Suggest two things the family could do to make the clothes dry faster indoors, explain why each would work, and state one factor they cannot change indoors that would have helped outdoors.

fuzzyTraps.vague: put a fan so it blows the water away
fuzzyTraps.precise: moving air removes water vapour from around the clothes, increasing the rate of evaporation

chain.text: Switch on a fan to blow air over the clothes.
Moving air carries away water vapour, increasing the rate of evaporation.
Spread the clothes out rather than bunching them.
A larger exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
Indoors they cannot give the clothes direct sunlight, which would supply far more heat energy.

questions.modelAnswer: The family could switch on a fan so that air moves over the clothes. Moving air carries away the water vapour near the wet cloth, which increases the rate of evaporation. They could also spread the clothes out instead of bunching them together, which increases the exposed surface area of the wet cloth and also increases the rate of evaporation. The one thing they cannot provide indoors is direct sunlight. Outdoors the clothes would gain much more heat energy from the sun, and the greater the heat energy gained, the higher the rate of evaporation.
markPoints: First workable suggestion
Its reason linked to rate of evaporation
Second workable suggestion
Its reason linked to rate of evaporation
Direct sunlight named as the missing factor, linked to heat energy
questions.whyMarksLost: Every reason in this question must land on the phrase rate of evaporation. Three separate ideas are being asked for, so a two-part answer cannot reach five marks however well written.

questions.commandDemand: Read the evidence given and state the conclusion it supports. Quote the evidence, then state what it shows.
questions.stimulus:
Four identical wet cloths were left in different places. The time taken for each to dry completely was recorded.

Cloth W, shaded and still air: 300 minutes
Cloth X, shaded and windy: 180 minutes
Cloth Y, sunny and still air: 140 minutes
Cloth Z, sunny and windy: 80 minutes
questions.stem: What can you infer about the conditions that affect how quickly water evaporates? Support each conclusion by naming the two cloths you compared and saying why that pair is a fair comparison.

fuzzyTraps.precise: both greater heat energy and moving air increase the rate of evaporation

chain.text: W and Y differ only in sunlight, and the sunny cloth dried faster.
More heat energy increases the rate of evaporation.
W and X differ only in air movement, and the windy cloth dried faster.
Moving air increases the rate of evaporation.

questions.modelAnswer: Comparing Cloth W with Cloth Y is a fair comparison because only the sunlight differs between them; the cloth in the sun dried faster, which shows that more heat energy increases the rate of evaporation. Comparing Cloth W with Cloth X is also fair because only the air movement differs; the windy cloth dried faster, which shows that moving air increases the rate of evaporation. Cloth Z cannot be used on its own for either conclusion, because both factors differ between it and Cloth W.
markPoints: More heat energy increases the rate of evaporation
Supported by the W and Y pair, where only sunlight differs
Moving air increases the rate of evaporation
Supported by the W and X pair, where only air movement differs
questions.whyMarksLost: Two of the four marks are for naming the pair and saying why it is fair. Reaching the right conclusion from the wrong comparison scores half.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism. The answer must connect the observation to the water cycle.
questions.stimulus: A gardener covers a potted plant with a clear plastic bag. After a day, droplets of water are seen on the inside of the bag.
questions.stem: Explain how the water droplets got onto the inside of the plastic bag, and state where that water was before the bag was put on.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the plant loses water vapour through transpiration

fuzzyTraps.vague: the water stuck to the bag
fuzzyTraps.precise: the water vapour condensed on the cooler surface of the bag

chain.text: The water was taken in from the soil by the roots and carried up to the leaves.
The plant lost it as water vapour through its leaves by transpiration.
The trapped water vapour lost heat energy at the cooler bag surface and condensed.

questions.modelAnswer: The water was originally in the soil, and it was absorbed by the roots and carried up through the plant to the leaves. The plant then lost it as water vapour through its leaves by transpiration. The water vapour was trapped inside the plastic bag, and when it came into contact with the cooler surface of the bag it lost heat energy and condensed, changing into liquid water droplets on the inside of the bag.
markPoints: The water came from the soil, absorbed by the roots
It left the leaves as water vapour by transpiration
It condensed on the cooler surface of the bag
questions.whyMarksLost: Tracing the water back to the soil is the extra mark here, and it is the one that shows you understand the plant as a system rather than a box that makes water.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the properties of the state of matter.
questions.stimulus: A helium balloon is squeezed. Its shape changes, but the amount of gas inside stays the same.
questions.stem: Explain why the gas inside the balloon can change shape when squeezed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a gas has no definite shape
a gas takes the shape of its container

chain.text: A gas has no definite shape.
It takes the shape of whatever container holds it.
When the balloon is squeezed the gas fills the new shape of the balloon.

questions.modelAnswer: A gas has no definite shape. It takes the shape of the container it is in. When the balloon is squeezed, the gas inside fills the new shape of the balloon, so its shape changes even though the amount of gas stays the same.
markPoints: A gas has no definite shape
A gas takes the shape of its container
questions.whyMarksLost: Answers about the balloon being stretchy describe the rubber, not the gas. The question asks about the gas, so the answer must use the properties of a gas.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using a property that distinguishes the two states.
questions.stimulus: Water is poured from a tall narrow jug into a wide flat dish. A wooden block is moved from the jug to the dish.
questions.stem: Explain why the water changes shape but the wooden block does not.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a liquid has no definite shape
a solid has a definite shape

chain.text: Water is a liquid, and a liquid has no definite shape.
The block is a solid, and a solid has a definite shape.
The liquid takes the shape of its container; the solid keeps its own shape.

questions.modelAnswer: Water is a liquid. A liquid has no definite shape and takes the shape of the container it is poured into, so it spreads out in the wide dish. The wooden block is a solid. A solid has a definite shape of its own, so it does not change shape when moved into the dish.
markPoints: A liquid has no definite shape and takes the shape of its container
A solid has a definite shape of its own
questions.whyMarksLost: Both halves are needed. Explaining only the water leaves the second mark unclaimed, because the question compares two things.

questions.commandDemand: State what is observed at each stage. The order matters.
questions.stimulus: A block of ice is taken from the freezer, left on a table until it melts, then heated in a pan until it boils away.
questions.stem: Describe the changes of state that the water goes through, name each change, and explain why the temperature does not rise while the ice is melting.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the ice melts, changing from the solid state to the liquid state
the water boils, changing from the liquid state to the gaseous state

chain.text: The ice gains heat energy and melts from solid to liquid.
During melting the heat energy gained is used to change the state, not to raise the temperature.
Once all the ice has melted, further heat energy raises the temperature of the liquid water.
At its boiling point the water boils, changing from liquid to water vapour.
Solid to liquid is melting; liquid to gas is boiling.

questions.modelAnswer: The ice gains heat energy from the surroundings and melts, changing from the solid state into the liquid state. While it is melting the temperature stays at its melting point, because the heat energy gained is used to change the state from solid to liquid rather than to raise the temperature. Once all the ice has melted, the heat energy gained raises the temperature of the liquid water. When the water reaches its boiling point it boils, changing from the liquid state into the gaseous state as water vapour.
markPoints: Melting: solid to liquid, gaining heat energy
Temperature stays constant during melting
Because the heat energy is used to change the state, not raise the temperature
After melting, further heat energy raises the temperature
Boiling: liquid to gas at the boiling point
questions.whyMarksLost: The heart of this question is that energy is still going in while the reading does not move. Writing that the heat 'stops working' is marked wrong.

questions.commandDemand: Use the data to reach a conclusion. Point at the evidence in the table.
questions.stimulus:
A student measured the volume and the shape of three substances after moving each into differently shaped containers.

Substance P: shape changed, volume stayed the same
Substance Q: shape stayed the same, volume stayed the same
Substance R: shape changed, volume changed to fill the container
questions.stem: Infer the state of matter of substances P, Q and R. Give a reason for each.

fuzzyTraps.vague: R is a gas because it spreads
fuzzyTraps.precise: R is a gas because it has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume

chain.text: No definite shape but a definite volume, so P is a liquid.
Definite shape and definite volume, so Q is a solid.
Neither definite shape nor definite volume, so R is a gas.

questions.modelAnswer: P is a liquid, because it has no definite shape but has a definite volume. Q is a solid, because it has both a definite shape and a definite volume. R is a gas, because it has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume and fills its container completely.
markPoints: P identified as a liquid, with no definite shape but a definite volume
Q identified as a solid, with definite shape and definite volume
R identified as a gas, with neither definite shape nor definite volume
questions.whyMarksLost: One mark per substance, and each needs its own reason in the language of definite shape and definite volume. Naming all three with a single shared reason scores one.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. The answer must refer to mass and to the fact that matter is conserved.
questions.stimulus: A sealed bottle containing ice is weighed. The ice is left to melt completely, and the sealed bottle is weighed again.
questions.stem: Explain why the mass of the sealed bottle stays the same after the ice melts. Predict and explain what would happen to the mass if the cap were left off and the bottle were left in a warm room for a week.

fuzzyTraps.precise: no matter entered or left the sealed bottle

fuzzyTraps.vague: it is still the same water
fuzzyTraps.precise: melting is a change of state, so the amount of matter is unchanged

chain.text: No matter can enter or leave the sealed bottle.
Melting is only a change of state, so the amount of matter is unchanged.
With the cap off, the water can evaporate into the surrounding air.
Matter leaves the bottle as water vapour, so the mass decreases.

questions.modelAnswer: The bottle is sealed, so no matter can enter or leave it. Melting is only a change of state from solid to liquid; it does not create or destroy matter, so the amount of matter inside is unchanged and the mass stays the same. If the cap were left off, the liquid water would gain heat energy in the warm room and evaporate into water vapour, which would escape into the surrounding air. Matter would then be leaving the bottle, so the mass of the bottle would decrease over the week.
markPoints: No matter enters or leaves the sealed bottle
A change of state does not change the amount of matter, so mass is unchanged
With the cap off the water evaporates into the air
Matter leaves the bottle, so the mass decreases
questions.whyMarksLost: The second half is the test of whether the first half was understood. If mass is unchanged only because nothing can get out, then opening the bottle must change it.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable method and say why it works.
questions.stimulus: A student is given a sealed box and told it contains one substance. She is not allowed to open it, but she may tilt it and weigh it.
questions.stem: Suggest how the student could find out whether the substance inside is a solid or a liquid.

fuzzyTraps.precise: tilt it and observe whether the contents flow to take the new shape

chain.text: Tilt the box slowly and feel or listen for the contents moving.
A liquid has no definite shape and will flow to fill the lower part of the box.
A solid keeps its definite shape and will not flow.

questions.modelAnswer: The student could tilt the box slowly and observe whether the contents shift to fill the lower part. A liquid has no definite shape and will flow to take the shape of the container as it is tilted. A solid has a definite shape and will not flow, so if the contents do not shift the substance is a solid.
markPoints: A workable test based on tilting the box
Reason given using definite shape, with what each result would mean
questions.whyMarksLost: A method without a prediction of what each outcome means is incomplete. Say what a liquid would do and what a solid would do.

questions.commandDemand: Give both similarities and differences, and make each point about both things.
questions.stem: Compare the properties of a liquid and a gas, and explain why a gas can be squeezed into a smaller container while a liquid cannot.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a gas has no definite volume, while a liquid has a definite volume

chain.text: Both have no definite shape and take the shape of their container.
A liquid has a definite volume; a gas does not.
A gas spreads out to fill its container completely, while a liquid occupies only part of it.
Because a gas has no definite volume it can be squeezed into a smaller space; a liquid keeps its volume and cannot.

questions.modelAnswer: Both a liquid and a gas have no definite shape, and both take the shape of the container they are in. However, a liquid has a definite volume while a gas has no definite volume. This means a gas spreads out and fills its container completely, whereas a liquid only occupies the lower part of the container. Because a gas has no definite volume, it can be squeezed into a container of smaller volume. A liquid has a definite volume that does not change, so it cannot be squeezed into a smaller space.
markPoints: Similarity: neither has a definite shape; both take the shape of the container
Difference: a liquid has a definite volume, a gas does not
A gas fills its container completely, a liquid does not
A gas can be compressed because it has no definite volume; a liquid cannot
questions.whyMarksLost: Compare means both, and the last mark needs the property applied to a new situation. Listing differences without using them to explain the squeezing stops at three.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, and refer to both animals in each point.
questions.stem: Compare the life cycle of a butterfly with the life cycle of a grasshopper, and explain why the young grasshopper competes with the adult for food while the young butterfly does not.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis, with a pupa stage
the nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and lacks wings

chain.text: Both begin as an egg and both undergo metamorphosis.
The butterfly has four stages including a pupa; the grasshopper has three and no pupa.
The nymph resembles the adult grasshopper, while the larva looks nothing like the adult butterfly.
The nymph eats the same food as the adult grasshopper, so they compete; the larva and adult butterfly eat different foods, so they do not.

questions.modelAnswer: Both the butterfly and the grasshopper begin life as an egg and both undergo metamorphosis. However, the butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis with four stages, egg, larva, pupa and adult, while the grasshopper undergoes incomplete metamorphosis with three stages, egg, nymph and adult. The grasshopper nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and has no wings, and it feeds on the same food as the adult, so the two stages compete with each other for the same food source. The butterfly larva looks completely different from the adult and feeds on leaves while the adult feeds on nectar, so the two stages do not compete.
markPoints: Similarity: both start as an egg and undergo metamorphosis
Difference: complete metamorphosis with a pupa versus incomplete with a nymph
The nymph eats the same food as the adult grasshopper, so they compete
The butterfly larva and adult eat different foods, so they do not compete
questions.whyMarksLost: The last two marks are the reason the two life cycles matter, not just how they differ. A comparison that never reaches competition has described without explaining.

questions.commandDemand: Give the advantage and say why it is an advantage for survival.
questions.stimulus: A butterfly larva feeds on leaves. The adult butterfly feeds on nectar from flowers.
questions.stem: Explain how this difference in diet is an advantage to the butterfly, and state one other advantage of the larva and the adult living in different ways.

fuzzyTraps.vague: they do not fight over food
fuzzyTraps.precise: they do not compete with each other for the same food source

chain.text: The larva and the adult eat different foods.
They therefore do not compete with each other for the same food source.
More of both stages obtain enough food and survive.
They also occupy different places, so a shortage or a danger in one place does not affect both stages.

questions.modelAnswer: The larva and the adult butterfly feed on different food sources, so they do not compete with each other for the same food. More individuals at both stages are therefore able to obtain enough food, which increases their chance of survival. A further advantage is that the two stages live in different places, the larva on the leaves and the adult in flight, so a shortage of food or a danger affecting one stage does not wipe out the other.
markPoints: The larva and adult do not compete for the same food source
This increases the chance of survival of both stages
A second valid advantage, such as not competing for space or being less easily wiped out by one problem
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark is for a genuinely different advantage, not the same one reworded. Competition for space is a different idea from competition for food.

questions.commandDemand: Use the data to identify the animal type or stage, and justify from the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
A scientist recorded the stages of four animals.

Animal A: egg, larva, pupa, adult
Animal B: egg, nymph, adult
Animal C: egg, young, adult, with the young hatching in water and later growing legs
Animal D: young born alive, adult
questions.stem: Infer which animal is most likely to be a frog, give a reason, and state which of the other animals undergoes complete metamorphosis.

fuzzyTraps.precise: C hatches in water as a tadpole and later develops legs, matching a frog's life cycle

chain.text: Animal C hatches from an egg in water and later grows legs.
A frog hatches as a tadpole in water and develops legs as it matures.
Animal A has egg, larva, pupa and adult, which is complete metamorphosis.

questions.modelAnswer: Animal C is most likely the frog. A frog lays eggs in water and the young hatch as tadpoles which live in water, and as the tadpole matures it develops legs and becomes an adult frog, which matches the stages recorded for Animal C. Animal A undergoes complete metamorphosis, because its life cycle has four stages, egg, larva, pupa and adult, and the pupa stage is what makes metamorphosis complete.
markPoints: Animal C identified as the frog
Reason linked to hatching in water and later developing legs, as a tadpole does
Animal A undergoes complete metamorphosis, shown by its four stages including a pupa
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark checks that you can read the whole table rather than only the row you were asked about.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason based on the life cycle.
questions.stimulus: A farmer sprays a chemical on his crops that kills only the larvae of a particular moth. The adult moths are unharmed.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the number of adult moths over the next few months and explain why. Suggest one reason why the number might not fall as much as expected.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the number of adult moths will decrease

fuzzyTraps.vague: the babies die so no more come
fuzzyTraps.precise: the larvae cannot develop into adults, so fewer adults are produced

chain.text: The number of adult moths will decrease.
The larvae are killed before they can complete the life cycle.
Every adult must pass through the larval stage, so fewer larvae means fewer adults.
Some larvae may escape the chemical, or moths may fly in from untreated fields nearby.

questions.modelAnswer: The number of adult moths will decrease. The chemical kills the larvae, so fewer larvae survive to develop into pupae and then into adult moths. Since the adult stage can only be reached by passing through the larval stage, fewer adults will be produced over the next few months. The number might not fall as much as expected because some larvae may not come into contact with the chemical and will survive, or adult moths may fly in from nearby fields that were not sprayed.
markPoints: The number of adult moths decreases
Larvae are killed before they can develop into adults
Every adult must pass through the larval stage, so the cycle is broken
A sensible reason the fall is smaller, such as survivors or moths arriving from elsewhere
questions.whyMarksLost: The fourth mark rewards thinking past the obvious answer. Real populations are never sealed off, and examiners like students who notice that.

questions.commandDemand: State the stages in order and name each one.
questions.stem: Describe the life cycle of a mosquito, and explain why removing standing water is a more effective control than spraying adult mosquitoes.

fuzzyTraps.vague: it starts as a baby in water
fuzzyTraps.precise: the egg hatches into a larva which lives in water

chain.text: The adult lays eggs in stagnant water.
The eggs hatch into larvae, which live in the water.
Each larva becomes a pupa, and the adult finally emerges.
Removing the water stops eggs, larvae and pupae all at once, whereas spraying kills only the adults already flying.

questions.modelAnswer: The adult mosquito lays its eggs in stagnant water. The eggs hatch into larvae, which live in the water, and each larva then develops into a pupa before the adult mosquito emerges and flies away; this is complete metamorphosis with four stages. Removing standing water is more effective than spraying adults because three of the four stages, the egg, the larva and the pupa, all need water to survive. Removing it therefore stops the whole cycle at once, while spraying kills only the adults that are already flying and does nothing to the eggs and larvae that will replace them.
markPoints: All four stages named in order: egg, larva, pupa, adult
The eggs are laid in stagnant water and the larvae live in it
Removing water destroys the egg, larva and pupa stages together
Spraying kills only adults, leaving the earlier stages to replace them
questions.whyMarksLost: The comparison is where the marks are. Knowing the four stages is only useful here if you can say which of them the control method attacks.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical action and explain how it breaks the life cycle.
questions.stimulus: A neighbourhood has a problem with mosquitoes. Residents are asked to help reduce the mosquito population.
questions.stem: Suggest one action residents could take, and explain how it would reduce the number of mosquitoes.

fuzzyTraps.precise: remove stagnant water so the larvae cannot develop

chain.text: Remove or empty any containers holding stagnant water.
Mosquitoes lay eggs in stagnant water and the larvae need water to develop.
Without stagnant water the life cycle is broken and fewer adults emerge.

questions.modelAnswer: Residents could empty any containers holding stagnant water, such as flower pot trays. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in stagnant water, and the larvae and pupae need water to develop. Without stagnant water the eggs cannot hatch and develop, so the life cycle is broken and fewer adult mosquitoes are produced.
markPoints: Practical action: remove or empty stagnant water
Explanation linked to the larval stage needing water, breaking the life cycle
questions.whyMarksLost: Suggesting the action without explaining which stage it attacks scores one mark. Name the stage that depends on the water.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the idea of a stage that does not feed or move.
questions.stimulus: A student watching a caterpillar notices it stops eating and becomes still inside a hard case for two weeks. It then emerges as a butterfly.
questions.stem: Explain what is happening inside the hard case during those two weeks, and state why the insect does not need to feed during this stage.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it is in the pupa stage, undergoing metamorphosis
its body structures are reorganised into those of the adult

chain.text: The hard case is the pupa stage of the life cycle.
Inside the pupa the larva's body undergoes metamorphosis and develops into the adult.
It does not feed because it uses the food it stored while it was a larva.

questions.modelAnswer: The hard case is the pupa stage of the butterfly's life cycle. Inside the pupa, the larva undergoes metamorphosis: its body structures are broken down and reorganised into those of the adult, such as wings and legs. The insect does not need to feed during this stage because it uses the food it took in and stored while it was a larva, which is why the larva spends so much of its time eating.
markPoints: The stage is named as the pupa
Metamorphosis occurs, developing the adult body structures
It uses food stored during the larval stage, so it does not need to feed
questions.whyMarksLost: Linking the pupa back to the larva's eating explains why the larva stage exists at all, and it is the mark that separates a memorised answer from an understood one.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. Link the structure to the method of dispersal.
questions.stimulus: A seed has a light, papery wing attached to one side.
questions.stem: Explain how this seed is dispersed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it is carried away by the wind
the wing increases the surface area, so the wind can carry it further

chain.text: The seed has a light, papery wing.
The wing increases the surface area while the seed stays light.
The wind can carry the seed further from the parent plant.

questions.modelAnswer: The seed is dispersed by wind. The light, papery wing increases the surface area of the seed while keeping it light. This allows the seed to be carried by the wind and blown further away from the parent plant.
markPoints: Dispersed by wind
The wing increases surface area and the seed is light, so it is carried further
questions.whyMarksLost: Saying 'by wind' alone is one mark. The second mark is for linking the structure, the wing, to the property that makes wind dispersal work.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. This is about competition, so the word must appear.
questions.stem: Explain why it is an advantage for a plant if its seeds are dispersed far away from the parent plant, and explain why a plant that produces very many seeds still has few that grow into adult plants.

fuzzyTraps.precise: they do not compete with the parent plant for space
there is less competition for water and mineral salts

chain.text: Seeds landing far away do not compete with the parent or each other.
They have more sunlight, water, mineral salts and space available.
Most seeds still land where conditions are unsuitable, or are eaten.
Only a few reach a place with the conditions needed to germinate and grow.

questions.modelAnswer: If the seeds land far from the parent plant, the seedlings do not have to compete with the parent or with one another for sunlight, water, mineral salts and space, so more of them can obtain what they need and grow successfully. Even so, few seeds become adult plants, because most land in places where the conditions are unsuitable for germination, for example where there is no water or no soil, and many are eaten by animals before they can germinate. Only the few that land somewhere with the right conditions survive to become adult plants.
markPoints: Less competition with the parent plant and other seedlings
Named resources: sunlight, water, mineral salts or space
Most seeds land where conditions are unsuitable for germination
Many are eaten or destroyed, so only a few survive to become adults
questions.whyMarksLost: The second half asks you to argue against your own first half. Producing many seeds is the plant's answer to a low survival rate, and saying so is what earns the last two marks.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and state which factor is needed, quoting the comparison.
questions.stimulus:
Four sets of identical seeds were placed in different conditions for one week.

Set 1, moist cotton wool, warm, in light: germinated
Set 2, dry cotton wool, warm, in light: did not germinate
Set 3, moist cotton wool, warm, in darkness: germinated
Set 4, moist cotton wool, in a fridge, in light: did not germinate
questions.stem: What can you infer about the conditions needed for germination? Support each conclusion by naming the two sets you compared.

fuzzyTraps.precise: seeds need water and warmth, but not light

chain.text: Sets 1 and 2 differ only in water, and only the moist set germinated.
Sets 1 and 4 differ only in temperature, and only the warm set germinated.
Set 3 germinated in darkness, so light is not needed.
Each pair is a fair comparison because only one factor differs between them.

questions.modelAnswer: Seeds need water and warmth for germination, but they do not need light. Comparing Set 1 with Set 2 is a fair comparison because only the water differs; only the moist set germinated, so water is needed. Comparing Set 1 with Set 4 is fair because only the temperature differs; only the warm set germinated, so warmth is needed. Set 3 was kept in darkness and still germinated, which shows that light is not needed. In each case only one factor was different between the two sets being compared, which is why each conclusion can be trusted.
markPoints: Water is needed, supported by comparing Sets 1 and 2
Warmth is needed, supported by comparing Sets 1 and 4
Light is not needed, supported by Set 3 germinating in darkness
Each comparison identified as fair because only one factor differs
questions.whyMarksLost: Adding light to the list because Set 1 had light is the classic error, and Set 3 is in the table specifically to catch it.

questions.commandDemand: State the stages in order.
questions.stem: Describe the life cycle of a flowering plant, starting from the seed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the seed germinates

chain.text: The seed germinates and grows into a seedling.
The seedling grows into an adult plant which produces flowers.
The flowers are pollinated and produce fruits with seeds, which are dispersed.

questions.modelAnswer: The seed germinates and grows into a seedling. The seedling grows into an adult plant, which then produces flowers. After pollination and fertilisation, the flowers develop into fruits containing seeds. These seeds are dispersed and can germinate to begin the cycle again.
markPoints: Germination into a seedling, then growth into an adult plant that flowers
Flowers produce seeds which are dispersed and germinate, completing the cycle
questions.whyMarksLost: The word germinates is worth having. 'The seed grows into a plant' skips the named process the examiner is checking for.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens and give the reason from the plant's needs.
questions.stimulus: A gardener sows fifty seeds very close together in a small pot. All of them germinate.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the seedlings as they grow and explain why. Suggest what the gardener should have done differently.

fuzzyTraps.precise: they will compete with one another for resources
some seedlings will grow poorly or die

chain.text: Many of the seedlings will grow poorly, and some will die.
They compete for limited sunlight, water and mineral salts.
Sowing fewer seeds or spacing them out would reduce the competition.

questions.modelAnswer: Many of the seedlings will grow poorly and some will die. Because they are sown very close together in a small pot, the seedlings compete with one another for sunlight, water and mineral salts, and there is not enough of these for all fifty. The gardener should have sown far fewer seeds in that pot, or spaced them further apart in a larger container, so that each seedling could obtain enough of the resources it needs.
markPoints: Some seedlings grow poorly or die
Reason: competition for named limited resources
The gardener should have sown fewer seeds, or spaced them further apart, or used a larger pot
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark is for a fix that actually reduces competition. Watering more does not help if the limiting resource is sunlight or space.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the fruit to its method of dispersal.
questions.stimulus: A fruit is brightly coloured, sweet and fleshy, and contains hard seeds that are not digested by animals.
questions.stem: Explain how the seeds of this fruit are dispersed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: animals eat the fruit and the seeds pass out in their droppings

chain.text: The fruit is brightly coloured and sweet, which attracts animals.
Animals eat the fruit, and the hard seeds are not digested.
The seeds pass out in the animals' droppings away from the parent plant.

questions.modelAnswer: The seeds are dispersed by animals. The bright colour and sweet, fleshy fruit attract animals to eat it. The hard seeds are not digested, so they pass out of the animal in its droppings at a place away from the parent plant, where they can germinate.
markPoints: Dispersed by animals, attracted by the colour or sweetness
Seeds are not digested and pass out in droppings away from the parent plant
questions.whyMarksLost: The detail that the seeds are not digested is the mark most often missed. It is the reason the seed survives the journey.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable design and justify it with the dispersal method.
questions.stimulus: A student is asked to design a model seed that will travel as far as possible when dropped from a height in still air.
questions.stem: Suggest two features the model seed should have and explain why each helps. Suggest one way the student could test fairly which of two model seeds travels further.

fuzzyTraps.vague: make it float in the air
fuzzyTraps.precise: a large surface area increases air resistance so it falls slowly

chain.text: A large surface area, such as wings or hairs.
This increases air resistance, so it falls more slowly and stays airborne longer.
A low mass, so the seed is light and easily carried.
Release both from the same height in the same conditions and measure the horizontal distance travelled.

questions.modelAnswer: The model seed should have a large surface area, for example papery wings or fine hairs, which increases the air resistance acting on it so that it falls more slowly and stays in the air longer. It should also have a low mass, because a lighter seed is more easily carried by moving air and so travels further. To compare two model seeds fairly, the student should release both from exactly the same height in the same room with the same air movement, and measure the horizontal distance each one lands from the release point.
markPoints: Large surface area, with the reason linked to air resistance
Low mass, with the reason linked to being carried further
A fair test releasing both from the same height in the same conditions
The measurement stated: horizontal distance travelled
questions.whyMarksLost: The fair-test half is worth two of the four marks. A design question that never says what will be measured cannot score them.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens, naming the parts involved.
questions.stem: Describe what happens during pollination in a flowering plant, and state what must happen next before a seed can form.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the pollen moves to the flower
fuzzyTraps.precise: pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma

chain.text: Pollen grains are produced in the anther.
They are carried to the stigma by an agent such as an insect or the wind.
The pollen grain grows a tube to the ovule, and fertilisation follows before a seed can form.

questions.modelAnswer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma. The pollen grains are carried there by an agent of pollination, such as an insect or the wind. Before a seed can form, fertilisation must follow: the pollen grain grows a tube down to the ovule, and the male sex cell fuses with the female sex cell inside it.
markPoints: Transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma
Carried out by an agent such as insects or wind
Fertilisation must follow: the male and female sex cells fuse in the ovule
questions.whyMarksLost: Adding the next step is what makes this a three mark answer. Pollination on its own produces nothing.

questions.commandDemand: Link each feature to how it helps that method of pollination.
questions.stimulus: Flower P has large, brightly coloured petals and produces a sweet scent and nectar. Flower Q has small, dull, unscented petals and produces large amounts of light pollen.
questions.stem: Explain which flower is pollinated by insects and which by wind.

fuzzyTraps.vague: P is pretty so insects like it
fuzzyTraps.precise: the bright petals, scent and nectar attract insects

fuzzyTraps.vague: Q has lots of pollen so wind blows it
fuzzyTraps.precise: large amounts of light pollen are easily carried by the wind

chain.text: Bright petals, scent and nectar attract insects, so P is insect pollinated.
Dull, unscented flowers do not attract insects.
Large amounts of light pollen are easily carried away by the wind, so Q is wind pollinated.

questions.modelAnswer: Flower P is pollinated by insects. Its large, brightly coloured petals, sweet scent and nectar attract insects, which pick up pollen and carry it to another flower. Flower Q is pollinated by wind. Its small, dull and unscented petals do not attract insects, and it produces large amounts of light pollen that can easily be carried away by moving air.
markPoints: P is insect pollinated, with features linked to attracting insects
Q is wind pollinated, with light or plentiful pollen linked to being carried by air
questions.whyMarksLost: Identifying both flowers with no feature linked to a reason scores one mark. Each identification needs its own justification.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and explain using the reproduction process.
questions.stimulus: A farmer grows an orchard of fruit trees inside a large sealed greenhouse. No insects can enter, and there is no wind inside.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the number of fruits produced and explain why. Suggest what the farmer could do to solve the problem without opening the greenhouse.

fuzzyTraps.precise: without an agent of pollination, pollen cannot be transferred to the stigma

chain.text: Very few or no fruits will be produced.
There is no insect or moving air to act as an agent of pollination.
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, and fruits form only after fertilisation.
Release insects inside, or transfer pollen from anther to stigma by hand.

questions.modelAnswer: Very few or no fruits will be produced. There are no insects and no moving air inside the sealed greenhouse to act as agents of pollination, so pollen grains cannot be transferred from the anther to the stigma. Without pollination, fertilisation cannot take place, and fruits only develop after fertilisation has occurred. To solve this without opening the greenhouse, the farmer could release insects such as bees inside it, or transfer the pollen himself from the anther to the stigma using a small brush.
markPoints: Few or no fruits produced
No agent of pollination, so pollen is not transferred from anther to stigma
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, so no fruits form
A workable solution: introduce insects or hand pollinate
questions.whyMarksLost: The chain has three links, no agent, no pollination, no fertilisation, and each is a mark. Jumping from 'no bees' to 'no fruit' collapses three marks into one.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical solution and explain the mechanism by which it works.
questions.stimulus: The same farmer wants his sealed greenhouse to produce fruit without opening it to the outside.
questions.stem: Suggest what the farmer could do, and explain how it would work.

fuzzyTraps.precise: introduce insects into the greenhouse to act as agents of pollination

chain.text: Introduce insects such as bees into the greenhouse, or pollinate the flowers by hand.
This transfers pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
Pollination allows fertilisation, so fruits can develop.

questions.modelAnswer: The farmer could release insects such as bees into the greenhouse, or transfer the pollen himself using a small brush. Either method transfers pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the flowers. This allows pollination and then fertilisation to take place, so the flowers can develop into fruits.
markPoints: A workable method of transferring pollen, by insects or by hand
Explained as transfer from anther to stigma allowing fertilisation
questions.whyMarksLost: 'Use bees' alone is one mark. The explanation must say what the bees actually do, in the language of anther and stigma.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the function of the flower part named.
questions.stimulus: A student removes all the anthers from a flower bud before it opens, then covers the flower with a bag.
questions.stem: Explain why this flower will not produce any seeds.

fuzzyTraps.vague: there is nothing to make seeds
fuzzyTraps.precise: no pollen grains are produced, so pollination cannot occur

chain.text: The anthers, which produce pollen grains, have been removed.
The bag also prevents pollen from other flowers reaching the stigma.
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, so no seeds form.

questions.modelAnswer: The anthers produce the pollen grains, and they have been removed, so this flower has no pollen of its own. The bag also prevents pollen from any other flower from reaching the stigma. Without pollination, fertilisation cannot take place, so no seeds can be formed.
markPoints: No pollen available, because the anthers were removed and the bag blocks outside pollen
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, so no seeds form
questions.whyMarksLost: The bag matters. An answer that only mentions the removed anthers has not explained why pollen from elsewhere could not arrive.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both processes in each point.
questions.stem: Compare pollination and fertilisation in a flowering plant, and explain why a flower can be pollinated but still produce no seeds.

fuzzyTraps.precise: fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female sex cells, which occurs after pollination

chain.text: Both are stages of sexual reproduction and both involve the pollen grain.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma.
Fertilisation is the fusion of the male sex cell with the female sex cell in the ovule.
If the pollen fails to reach the ovule, fertilisation does not happen and no seeds form.

questions.modelAnswer: Both pollination and fertilisation are stages in the sexual reproduction of a flowering plant, and both involve the pollen grain. However, pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma, while fertilisation is the fusion of the male sex cell from the pollen grain with the female sex cell inside the ovule. A flower can be pollinated but still produce no seeds, because pollination only brings the pollen to the stigma. If the pollen grain does not grow a tube down to the ovule, the two sex cells never fuse, so fertilisation does not occur and no seeds are formed.
markPoints: Similarity: both are stages of sexual reproduction involving the pollen grain
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
Fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female sex cells in the ovule
Pollination alone is not enough; without fusion at the ovule no seeds form
questions.whyMarksLost: The last mark exists to test whether you really see them as two events. If pollination were enough, the second word would not be needed.

questions.commandDemand: Use the results to draw a conclusion, quoting which plants you are comparing.
questions.stimulus:
Four identical flowering plants were treated differently and the number of fruits produced was counted.

Plant 1, left uncovered outdoors: 24 fruits
Plant 2, covered with a fine mesh bag: 2 fruits
Plant 3, covered with a fine mesh bag, pollen brushed onto stigmas by hand: 21 fruits
Plant 4, anthers removed and left uncovered: 19 fruits
questions.stem: What can you infer from these results about how this plant is pollinated? Refer to each of the four plants in your answer.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the mesh bag prevented insects from reaching the flowers, so pollination did not occur

chain.text: Left uncovered outdoors, it fruited heavily, giving the normal result.
Bagged, it barely fruited, so something the bag blocked is needed.
Bagged but hand pollinated, it fruited nearly normally, so the missing step was pollen transfer.
Anthers removed yet still fruiting, so the pollen came from another plant.
An outside agent, most likely insects, carries pollen from another plant.

questions.modelAnswer: This plant relies on an outside agent, most likely insects, to carry pollen to it from another plant. Plant 1 was left uncovered and produced 24 fruits, which is the normal result. Plant 2 was bagged and produced almost none, showing that the bag blocked something the plant needs. Plant 3 was also bagged but had pollen brushed onto its stigmas by hand and produced 21 fruits, which shows that the missing step was the transfer of pollen to the stigma rather than anything else the bag prevented. Plant 4 had its anthers removed and still produced 19 fruits, which shows that the pollen must have come from a different plant.
markPoints: An external agent, most likely insects, transfers the pollen
Plant 2 shows something the bag blocks is needed
Plant 3 shows the missing step is specifically pollen transfer to the stigma
Plant 4 shows the pollen comes from another plant
Plant 1 identified as the normal comparison
questions.whyMarksLost: Five marks and four rows is a deliberate signal that every row is doing work. Plant 4 is the one most students skip, and it carries the hardest conclusion.
